2026-09-06.headline: NESA caps unsupervised HSC work at 15 per cent as New York pauses AI for students through Year 8, and the vendor race standardises on free access with system-wide privacy deals
2026-09-06.overview: The moratorium question NSW posed a month ago was answered this week: from Term 4, schools are limited to one take-home assessment task per HSC course worth no more than 15 per cent of school-based assessment, with major-works courses exempt, and the rules reach every school delivering the HSC. In the same week, New York City imposed the broadest school AI restriction in the United States, a one-year pause on student-facing generative AI through Grade 8 for nearly 600,000 students, with companion chatbots banned in every grade. Anthropic completed the vendor convergence by opening free, centrally managed Claude for Teachers to whole US school systems under a single K-12 data agreement, and UNESCO convenes 30 education ministers next week to adopt a statement on education as a common good in the age of AI. The pattern is unmistakable: student-facing use is being restricted by regulation at the same moment teacher-facing adoption is being accelerated by vendors.
signals: NSW announced that from Term 4 2026 schools may set only one take-home assessment task per HSC course, worth at most 15 per cent of the school-based assessment mark (7.5 per cent of the HSC), extending to Year 11 from 2027, with creative arts, technology and English Extension 2 major works exempt.

New York City announced on 2 September a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI from pre-kindergarten through Grade 8, covering nearly 600,000 students, alongside an all-grades companion chatbot ban, screen time limits and twice-yearly AI critical-thinking modules for high schoolers.

Anthropic made Claude for Teachers free for US K-12 schools and districts as a centrally managed Enterprise offering on 28 August, with a system-wide K-12 Data Processing Agreement and a Detroit Public Schools pilot evaluating effects on educator wellbeing and practice.
UNESCO's Digital Learning Week (8 to 11 September, Paris) will see around 30 education ministers adopt a joint statement on sustaining education as a common good in the age of AI.
South Australia's Royal Commission terms of reference, promised within four to six weeks of the 10 August announcement, are now due imminently, with commissioners commencing 1 October.
actions: Audit Year 11 and 12 assessment schedules against the new NESA limit before Term 4 begins on 12 October: confirm each HSC course has at most one take-home task within the 15 per cent cap, brief heads of major-works subjects on their exemptions, and watch for AISNSW guidance translating the rules for independent schools.

Use the NYC decision to pressure-test the school's own primary-years AI position: its student-facing versus teacher-facing distinction, outright companion chatbot ban, and paired critical-thinking instruction form a coherent reference model, and the criticism it drew previews the parent objections any local restriction would need answers for.

Fold Anthropic's free Enterprise offer into the standing vendor question rather than evaluating it alone: with all three majors now offering free teacher access under system-level privacy agreements, the item worth raising with ISA or AISNSW is a sector-negotiated Australian equivalent, and the exit cost when free periods end.

2026-08-30.headline: National Cabinet locks in AI legislation for 2027 as every education department converges on supervised assessment, and the school photo question turns from advice into action
2026-08-30.overview: The national AI regulatory picture firmed this week: National Cabinet on 26 August backed the Commonwealth's plan to legislate national AI laws and mandatory data centre standards from early 2027, while an ABC national scan showed every education department moving assessment back under supervision, with no system betting on AI detection. In the ACT, the eSafety Commissioner's school imagery advisory started changing visible practice, with at least one Canberra school stripping every photo from its website. Internationally, OpenAI expanded free ChatGPT for Teachers past 300,000 US educators under a first-of-its-kind 16-state privacy agreement, and a Bocconi randomised trial found ChatGPT lifts the quality of student work but not its originality, while critical-thinking training does the reverse. The through-line is that governance is hardening while the vendor land-grab for teachers accelerates.
signals: National Cabinet on 26 August affirmed the Commonwealth's plan to legislate national AI laws and mandatory standards for large data centres across all nine governments, with legislation intended in early 2027.

ABC's 25 August national scan found every state education department is tightening AI cheating responses, led by NSW's proposed moratorium on unsupervised take-home assessment now awaiting NESA advice due before Term 4 begins on 12 October.

A Canberra Times feature on 29 August reported at least one Canberra Catholic school has removed all photographs from its website in response to eSafety's school imagery advisory, leaving a single image of an empty playground.

OpenAI announced on 26 August that 55 more US school systems are adopting free ChatGPT for Teachers, passing 100 K-12 organisations and 300,000 educators, under a 16-state National Data Privacy Agreement it calls a first for the industry.

A randomised trial of more than 1,000 Bocconi undergraduates found ChatGPT access lifted work quality by nearly a full rubric point but did not increase originality, while critical-thinking training produced unique ideas without improving scores; only students with both showed both effects.
actions: Adjust assessment schedules on the assumption that supervised demonstration of learning becomes the default this term: the ABC scan gives the executive a documented national trend to cite, and NESA's advice in September will set the benchmark independent schools are measured against.

Take a deliberate, minuted position on student imagery before parents raise the empty playground story: decide what goes on the open web versus authenticated portals, confirm consent settings cover AI misuse, and agree the response plan for a deepfake report.

Treat every free vendor offer reaching staff, including Microsoft Elevate and any ChatGPT for Teachers equivalent, as a procurement decision with an exit cost: the useful precedent to raise with ISA or AISNSW is OpenAI's sector-wide privacy agreement, negotiated once for many schools rather than school by school.

2026-08-16.headline: NSW moves to end unsupervised assessment as South Australia calls the nation's first AI royal commission, and the pastoral blind spot around AI companions widens
2026-08-16.overview: Australian AI policy hardened in a single week: NSW asked NESA to consider a moratorium on unsupervised take-home assessment tasks from Term 4 while it reviews AI's effect on learning, and South Australia announced the country's first Royal Commission into AI with education squarely in scope. Federal Education Minister Jason Clare reinforced the direction, framing learning integrity and student privacy as the centre of the national response. Internationally, Stateline documented US districts spending billions on AI tools they cannot evaluate, and clinicians published sobering evidence on teenagers quietly using AI chatbots for emotional support. The message across all of it is that governance is moving from guidance to machinery, and schools should position ahead of binding rules.
signals: NSW Deputy Premier Prue Car asked NESA to urgently consider a moratorium on unsupervised, take-home assessment tasks while a broader review of AI's impact on learning runs, with interim changes possible from the start of Term 4 2026 and major projects expected to need separate arrangements.

South Australia announced Australia's first Royal Commission into AI on 10 August, covering education alongside work and public services, with commissioners starting 1 October 2026 and a final report due by 1 July 2027.

Learning First's NSW survey behind the assessment debate found 80 per cent of lower secondary teachers who report student AI use say students use it to complete assessment tasks, and about half of secondary teachers do not know how to prevent AI-enabled plagiarism.

Stateline's 12 August investigation found US districts choosing among an average of 3,001 available digital tools while students and educators actively use about four, with little independent evidence or federal guidance for AI purchases.

UMass Chan clinicians report 72 per cent of US teens have used AI companion chatbots and 63 per cent of those seeking mental health advice from a chatbot told no one, while Linewize found 60 per cent of schools say students confide in AI instead of adults.
actions: Start contingency planning for Stage 6 assessment schedules now rather than waiting for NESA's advice: if the moratorium proceeds, supervised replacements for take-home tasks will need timetable space in Term 4, and the school should have an agreed position on the instructional-time trade-off before parents raise it.

Track the SA royal commission's terms of reference when they land next month and flag the submission window with the principal; a practising school's classroom evidence, routed directly or through ISA and AISNSW, will carry more weight than another peak-body position paper.

Brief wellbeing staff on the AI companion evidence and eSafety's information sheet, treating student reliance on AI chatbots as a disclosure pathway rather than a technology-use breach, and fold companionship (not just homework) into the next round of parent communication about AI.

2026-08-09.headline: Frontier chatbots fail the Australian curriculum test just as agentic AI reaches managed school accounts, and TALIS locates the capability gap squarely in primary
2026-08-09.overview: An Australian-first benchmark showed the leading AI models barely recall Australian and New Zealand curricula, with no mainstream model passing more than 41 per cent of curriculum-knowledge questions, in the same week OpenAI shipped education plugins that run agentic workflows over school-supplied materials. Coverage of ACER's TALIS 2024 Australian Report confirmed Australia ranks fourth of 55 systems for teacher AI use while half of primary teachers use none, overwhelmingly for lack of skills. In the US, Alpha Schools' expansion to 50 campuses and a Houston public-school pilot pushed AI-first schooling ahead of an evidence base that does not yet support it. National Cabinet's decision on the national AI standards had still not landed by week's end.
signals: CurricuLLM's benchmark of seven frontier models (including GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.5) found none exceeded a 41 per cent pass rate on Australian and NZ K-10 curriculum knowledge, with two scoring zero on identifying specific curriculum outcome entries.

ACER's TALIS 2024 Australian Report shows about two in three lower secondary but only one in two primary teachers used AI in the past year, and 84 per cent of primary non-users say they lack the knowledge or skills to teach with it.

The same survey found 87 per cent of lower secondary teachers are concerned AI lets students misrepresent others' work as their own, and two in five non-users believe schools should not use AI in teaching at all.

OpenAI released K-12 Educator, College Educator and College Student plugins for ChatGPT Work and Codex on 3-4 August, packaging agentic lesson-planning workflows that run on the course materials and context a school supplies.

Alpha Schools announced expansion from about a dozen to roughly 50 US campuses, and Houston ISD will pilot its Timeback platform in two public elementary schools, while a Conversation research review found no evidence AI tutors outperform human teachers.
actions: Fold the curriculum-recall benchmark into staff professional learning now: teachers should supply syllabus content to AI tools rather than trust model recall, and any AI-generated planning citing outcome codes needs checking against the source document.

Use the TALIS primary-years data to shape next term's PL priorities: the gap is skills, not resistance, so foundational capability-building for K-6 staff will land better than tool rollouts, and the integrity concern shared by 87 per cent of teachers is an open door for assessment-design work.

Review what any school-managed AI workspace can now do agentically, and settle the data governance question of what school materials may be uploaded to vendor platforms, before staff discover these workflows on their own.

2026-08-02.headline: eSafety turns the lens on schools' own photo streams as deepfake abuse escalates, and the first classroom RCT complicates the teacher time-saving story
2026-08-02.overview: The week belonged to the eSafety Commissioner, whose 28 July advisory on sharing school imagery reframed the routine publishing of student photos as a safeguarding exposure, after more than 100 reports in the first quarter of anonymous accounts weaponising imagery scraped from school websites and social media. Human Rights Watch amplified the warning two days later. Internationally, the first randomised controlled trial of a teacher-facing AI assistant found teachers saved time while student experience and, under weaker teachers, achievement declined, and the EU's AI transparency rules took legal effect on 2 August. National Cabinet's meeting on Australia's AI standards is now imminent.
signals: eSafety's 28 July advisory follows 100+ reports between January and March 2026 of anonymous accounts targeting schools with AI face swaps, fabricated stories and sexualised deepfakes built almost entirely from school-published imagery; it recommends a risk-based approach to collecting, approving, posting and storing images.
Human Rights Watch (30 July) tied the advisory to its 2024 finding that Australian children's photos appear in AI training datasets and called for stronger children's data-privacy protections.

A Wharton-led RCT of 193 teachers and 2,800+ students, circulated widely this week, found a ChatGPT-based teaching assistant saved teacher time but left students rating classes as less enjoyable, with achievement falling where previously weaker teachers used AI output unadapted.

Turnitin data analysed in The Conversation shows 53.6% of Australian tertiary submissions from October 2025 to April 2026 contained AI-assisted writing, with the authors cautioning that detection scores indicate likelihood, not misconduct.

The EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency obligations took effect on 2 August: chatbots must disclose they are AI and deepfakes must be labelled, while high-risk education obligations were deferred to December 2027.
actions: Commission an audit of the school's public photo footprint (website, social media, newsletters) against the eSafety advisory before the next marketing cycle, including consent language and an incident plan for deepfake abuse of students or staff.

Use the Wharton RCT to argue that every teacher-facing AI tool must ship with professional learning on curating and adapting output, and that pilots should track student experience data rather than teacher satisfaction alone.
Prepare a short principal briefing on the national AI standards ahead of National Cabinet's August meeting, so the school can respond on its own terms when the outcome lands.

2026-07-26.headline: A quiet week in Canberra, but AI companions consolidate as the next safeguarding frontier and parents converge with teachers on guardrails
2026-07-26.overview: With no new federal moves ahead of August's National Cabinet, the running was made by researchers and platforms. Australian academics analysed China's new AI companion law, in force since 15 July, in the same week the eSafety Commissioner ran educator training on companion chatbots and deepfakes. Instructure's 2026 survey shows parents, teachers and students now share the same top three AI concerns, and OpenAI let parents lock teen ChatGPT accounts to its Socratic Study Mode by default.
signals: China's AI companion law took effect on 15 July, forcing major companion services to restrict emotionally responsive chat; University of Tasmania and RMIT-linked researchers warned in The Conversation (23 July) of an AI-induced 'loneliness spiral' among young users.
The eSafety Commissioner ran a professional learning webinar for educators on 23 July covering AI companions, deepfakes, AI influencers and AI-facilitated cyberbullying.
Instructure's State of AI in Education 2026 survey (21 July) found 45% of K-12 educators have had no formal AI training, and only 8% call their training comprehensive.

The same survey found parents, educators and students share the same top concerns (overreliance, loss of critical thinking, integrity) and all accept AI for support tasks but not for grading decisions.
OpenAI's teen safety rollout lets parents make Study Mode the default for linked teen accounts, drawing a moratorium call from advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens.
actions: Treat AI companion use as a wellbeing and pastoral care matter now: brief wellbeing staff and consider the eSafety educator webinar series before an incident forces the issue.
Use the Instructure findings in parent communication; the community consensus on guardrails rather than bans makes this a good moment to socialise the school's AI position.
Note the parent-controlled Study Mode default when advising families: home AI use may already be more structured than school guidance assumes.

2026-07-19.headline: Canberra moves to legislate AI standards, education ministers target deepfakes, and the classroom platform race accelerates
2026-07-19.overview: The Prime Minister announced an Office of AI and legislated national standards that explicitly cover education and training, with a draft framework going to National Cabinet in August. On the same day, education ministers met in Parramatta, where Jason Clare called for national standards against AI-generated intimate images of students. Meanwhile, Turnitin data shows more than half of Australian university submissions now contain AI content, and Anthropic's Claude for Teachers joins an increasingly crowded race for teachers' habitual use.
signals: Australia will establish an Office of Artificial Intelligence within the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, with legislated national AI standards covering education to be presented at National Cabinet in August and legislation intended for early 2027.

Education Minister Jason Clare called for national standards to combat AI-generated non-consensual intimate images of students, describing deepfakes as 'the latest frontier of bullying'. Female students, and increasingly female teachers, are the main targets.

Turnitin data shows 53.6% of Australian tertiary submissions from October 2025 to April 2026 contained AI-generated content; Curtin University has disabled Turnitin's AI detection feature over reliability concerns.
Anthropic launched Claude for Teachers, free for verified US educators, with pre-built connectors including Canva Education and MagicSchool, both already common in Australian schools.
Day of AI Australia's UNSW partnership secured Google.org accelerator backing to build free, curriculum-aligned AI literacy experiences for Australian classrooms.
actions: Review the school's AI policy and platform data agreements ahead of August's National Cabinet meeting, on the working assumption that today's voluntary framework becomes binding standards in 2027.
Ensure the school's safeguarding response covers deepfake incidents targeting both students and staff, using the eSafety Commissioner's educator resources as the practical starting point.
Check whether the AI policy addresses platform-specific data agreements, since teachers often adopt tools informally through connector ecosystems before procurement processes catch up.

2026-07-12.headline: Questions over the national evidence base, a safeguarding escalation, and fresh proof that AI output is not the same as learning
2026-07-12.overview: A governance dispute over AERO's suppressed performance review raises questions about how much weight schools should place on national evidence bodies, while the eSafety Commissioner reports deepfake incidents involving under-18s have more than doubled. The OECD's flagship 2026 report and EDUtech keynotes converge on one message: what matters is not whether students use AI, but the pedagogical conditions under which they use it.
signals: The federal government has refused an FOI request for a KPMG evaluation of AERO, with AERO itself objecting to release. School leaders should weigh AERO resources alongside other peer-reviewed sources for now.
eSafety reports of digitally altered images of under-18s have more than doubled in 18 months; four in five involve female students. Enforcement against 'nudify' platforms is under way.
The OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 finds GenAI improves task performance without necessarily building knowledge, coining the term 'metacognitive disengagement'.
Professor Rose Luckin at EDUtech: catching students using AI is the wrong question; designing assessment where AI cannot substitute for thinking is the right one.
Microsoft's global survey: 92% of students have used AI for schoolwork, yet 77% have had no formal training.
actions: Confirm the school has a clear staff protocol for reporting deepfake incidents to eSafety, and brief pastoral care teams.
Frame any AI assessment policy around pedagogical conditions for productive use, not detection and enforcement.
Use the adoption-versus-training gap data to support the case for structured staff AI professional learning.

2026-07-05.headline: The strongest evidence yet that unstructured AI use erodes learning, and a five-month regulatory countdown for school AI tools
2026-07-05.overview: A landmark study of 3.2 million learning interactions documents 'cognitive surrender': high school students studying 31% less on AI-susceptible tasks with a 25% decline in retention, though notably no effect at the Year 5 level. Meanwhile the final Children's Online Privacy Code lands on 10 December, giving schools roughly five months to review every AI tool students touch.
signals: The 'Faster Completion, Less Learning' study shows retention losses concentrate in secondary years; primary students show no detectable effect yet, making the primary years the window to build AI-resistant learning habits.
The World Economic Forum argues the real divide is AI literacy, not access: 1 in 3 teachers uses AI while 3 in 4 feel unprepared to teach with it.
The OAIC's Children's Online Privacy Code is due 10 December 2026 and its 'likely accessed by children' scope will capture many general-purpose AI tools used in classrooms.
NSWEduChat's state-wide rollout offers a reference model: data kept in Australia, curriculum alignment, and guardrails that prompt reasoning rather than answers.
The Brookings Global Task Force, spanning 50 countries, concludes that under current conditions the risks of AI for students outweigh the benefits, while stopping short of recommending bans.
actions: Commission a review of all approved student-facing AI tools against the draft privacy code before the December deadline.
Benchmark any student AI tool against NSWEduChat's three design tests: data sovereignty, curriculum alignment, pedagogical guardrails.
Audit AI governance against Brookings' three pillars: Prosper, Prepare, Protect. Most schools over-invest in Protect.

2026-06-28.headline: National agencies move towards a single commission, while adoption data shows AI use has outrun training everywhere
2026-06-28.overview: The design proposal for a Teaching and Learning Commission merging ACARA, AITSL, AERO and ESA went to ministers this month, concentrating national AI-in-education policy in one future body. Microsoft's six-country survey, which includes Australia, finds 92% of students using AI while 77% have never been formally trained, and both Microsoft and Google announced AI features that will arrive inside platforms schools already run.
signals: The Teaching and Learning Commission would become the single national locus for curriculum, teacher standards, research and digital resources, and therefore for AI policy.
Microsoft's AI in Education Report: 92% of students and leaders use AI; 77% of students and 53% of educators report no formal training; most want regular training provided.
Google is embedding Gemini directly into Classroom, and Microsoft is adding free AI tools to 365 Education. AI will arrive via feature updates, not procurement decisions.
Stanford's SCALE review of 800+ studies finds only 20 causal ones; performance gains tend to fade when the AI is removed, except in tools with pedagogical guardrails.
52 AI-in-education bills are active across 25 US states, signalling where regulation in the English-speaking world is heading: mandatory school AI policies and limits on AI replacing teachers.
actions: Ensure AI governance covers feature updates to existing platforms (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365), not only new tool approvals.
Use the Microsoft training-gap data to justify structured AI professional learning in the next planning cycle.
Adopt a procurement question backed by the Stanford review: is this tool designed to support the learning process or just to produce output?

2026-06-21.headline: Free national teacher training matures, UK legislates on AI and children, and evidence emerges of bias in AI writing feedback
2026-06-21.overview: ESA and Microsoft released the second module of their free, nationally aligned AI professional learning series, moving from awareness to classroom implementation. A Stanford study found AI writing feedback tools systematically give less substantive critique to students identified as belonging to marginalised groups, and the UK passed the most direct AI-and-child-safety legislation in the English-speaking world.
signals: ESA Module 2 (AI Implementation) is free, aligned to the teacher standards and national framework, and counts towards professional development evidence.
Stanford's 'Marked Pedagogies' study: AI feedback tools praised more and critiqued less when essays were labelled as written by Black, Hispanic, Asian, female or learning-disabled students.
The UK's Children's Safety Act and AI Chatbot Powers Act give regulators explicit powers over AI chatbots that engage children, a model likely to influence Australian reform.
The OAIC's consultation drew 337 responses including 161 from primary-aged children, who clearly articulated wanting control and trust over their data.
eSafety hosted a free educator webinar on AI chatbots, deepfakes and AI-facilitated cyberbullying; the Children's Online Privacy Code consultation has now closed ahead of the December deadline.
actions: Offer the free ESA modules as the baseline layer of the staff AI professional learning programme.
Require an equity impact check before adopting any AI feedback or marking tool, with monitoring of outcomes by student cohort.
Ask edtech vendors what Children's Online Privacy Code compliance work is under way ahead of December.

2026-06-14.headline: Queensland puts a state-built AI in students' hands, free national teacher training arrives, and the metacognitive risk evidence hardens
2026-06-14.overview: Queensland's government-built Corella platform is now in every state high school and open to Years 7 to 10 students with parental consent, the most explicit government endorsement of student-facing AI in Australian schooling so far. Microsoft's free Elevate for Educators programme offers a nationally aligned AI credential for teachers, while new RAND survey data and a peer-reviewed scoping review sharpen the evidence that AI use can improve task output while weakening the thinking behind it.
signals: Queensland's Corella, a government-owned AI platform hosted on state infrastructure, has rolled out to all state high schools, with Year 7 to 10 student access available under parental consent.
Microsoft's Elevate for Educators gives all Australian teachers free AI training and a credential formally aligned with the national AI framework and the professional standards for teachers.
Iceland's national AI pilot concluded: teachers saved meaningful planning time, but the union-side review flagged dependency, data sovereignty and language-culture risks for other governments.
RAND: 63% of US high schoolers now use AI for homework, up 14 points in seven months, and 67% believe it harms their critical thinking; only one in three reports a school-wide rule.
A peer-reviewed scoping review finds offloading tasks to AI fosters 'metacognitive passivity' even where task performance improves, converging with OECD and Stanford findings.
actions: Audit the data governance arrangements of the commercial AI tools in use at the school against the benchmark Queensland has set with a government-hosted platform.
Evaluate Microsoft's free AI Literacy for Educators credential as a shared baseline for staff professional learning, while weighing its vendor perspective.
Treat metacognitive passivity as a working assumption in task design: any AI-assisted activity should preserve the cognitive effort that produces the learning.

2026-06-07.headline: Australia's biggest edtech event puts assessment redesign at the centre, as NSW data shows policy and student behaviour have parted ways
2026-06-07.overview: EDUtech Australia drew over 10,000 attendees with 'keeping humans in the loop' as the dominant theme. A Learning First survey of more than 4,000 NSW teachers found three-quarters of secondary teachers whose students use AI say it is being used to complete assessments despite restrictions, and half do not know how to prevent it. Stanford and the OECD both published sobering evidence on the gap between AI-assisted output and durable learning.
signals: EDUtech consensus: AI detection tools cannot reliably identify AI-generated work, shifting the integrity burden from surveillance to assessment design.
Learning First NSW survey: students are using AI to complete assessments even where restrictions formally apply. That is a design problem, not just a compliance problem.
Stanford's review of 1,100+ studies found only 20 meeting causal standards; gains during AI use are inconsistent once the AI is removed.
The OECD documents 'metacognitive laziness': students producing better outputs while doing less of the thinking the task was meant to develop.
eSafety has written to education ministers about mandatory reporting of deepfake incidents and released an updated Toolkit for Schools.
actions: Start an explicit audit of which assessments genuinely test student learning rather than AI capability.
Distribute the eSafety Toolkit for Schools to pastoral care and wellbeing teams.
Treat 'output quality' and 'learning' as separate outcomes in any evaluation of classroom AI use.

2026-05-31.headline: Half of NSW secondary teachers cannot prevent AI cheating, a children's privacy code nears, and teacher unions enter the debate
2026-05-31.overview: The largest Australian survey of educator attitudes to student AI use finds restrictions widely in place and widely ignored, and recommends restricting student access until durable learning benefits are demonstrated. The OAIC's Children's Online Privacy Code closes for consultation this week, with material consequences for how schools procure edtech, while America's largest teaching union calls for an end to student-facing AI in elementary schools and a levy on AI companies to fund teacher training.
signals: Learning First's survey of more than 4,000 NSW educators: around three-quarters of teachers whose students use AI report use in assessment tasks, despite over 80% saying their school has restrictions; about half say they cannot prevent AI-related plagiarism.
The report's central recommendation is the most restrictive position yet from a credible Australian body: restrict student AI access for schoolwork until research shows durable learning gains.
The OAIC Children's Online Privacy Code consultation closes 5 June; the final code, due by December, would tighten consent obligations for AI and edtech tools used with younger students.
The American Federation of Teachers' 10-point plan calls for no student-facing AI in elementary schools, no AI companions for under-16s, and a levy on AI companies to fund teacher training.
The EU Council adopted conclusions positioning teachers as designers and evaluators of classroom AI rather than passive users, a framing Australian policy has historically followed.
actions: Audit the gap between the school's written AI policy and actual student practice rather than assuming restrictions are being observed.
Confirm whether AISNSW is making a submission on the Children's Online Privacy Code, and review consent processes for AI-enabled tools used with younger students.
Prepare an evidence-based position on the restrict-versus-teach debate that the school can defend to parents on both sides of it.

2026-05-24.headline: The rules of the profession are being rewritten: teacher standards, a new national commission, and a mandatory AI integrity course
2026-05-24.overview: AITSL opened the first review of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers in 15 years, the Teaching and Learning Commission received budget funding, and Queensland made an AI-aware academic integrity course a formal requirement of the QCE. At the same time, data suggests Australian teachers' world-leading AI adoption is driven more by workload relief than pedagogy.
signals: The AITSL review (consultation to February 2027) is the formal mechanism through which AI capability could enter teacher accreditation requirements.
Queensland now requires an academic integrity course covering AI use as a condition of the QCE, the most concrete state assessment authority response so far.
Australian teachers rank among the highest AI users in the OECD, but the driver appears to be unsustainable marking loads rather than deliberate integration.
The Teaching and Learning Commission was funded in the May budget; design proposals are with ministers.
New research on students using AI chatbots for mental health support highlights accessibility benefits but serious safeguarding limits.
actions: Consider a school or staff submission to the AITSL standards review while the consultation window is open.
Diagnose what staff AI use actually looks like in practice before designing the next round of professional learning.
Set a clear school position on AI-powered wellbeing tools: useful for lowering barriers, never a substitute for clinical judgement.

2026-05-17.headline: Governments fund teacher-facing AI, a privacy code redraws the rules for school edtech, and AI detection lands in court
2026-05-17.overview: Western Australia committed $4.6 million to expand its ClassmAIte lesson-planning tool, while the federal budget channelled AI investment through commercial R&D rather than schools. The OAIC's draft Children's Online Privacy Code would require parental rather than school consent for many edtech tools used by under-15s, and a Californian family filed the first civil rights suit over an AI-detection false accusation.
signals: WA's ClassmAIte expansion is the first state programme with an independent schools association as a formal implementation partner, and it is teacher-facing by design.
The federal budget confirmed schools will largely self-fund AI adoption and professional learning; no national edtech quality assurance framework emerged.
The draft Children's Online Privacy Code would stop schools consenting to platforms on behalf of under-15s; consultation closes 5 June.
Research shows AI detectors flag non-native English writers at up to five times the rate of native speakers; the Palo Alto lawsuit shows the legal exposure that follows.
Parent communities are beginning to contest school AI decisions publicly, as seen in New York's demand for a moratorium.
actions: Audit the school's edtech stack against the draft privacy code, especially tools deployed year-group-wide on school-granted consent.
Review the academic integrity policy so that AI detection output can open a conversation but never close a case.
Prepare a transparent account of how the school makes and governs AI tool decisions, ready for parent questions.

2026-05-10.headline: A pillar of the pro-AI evidence base collapses, and the quiet normalisation of AI marking demands a policy answer
2026-05-10.overview: Nature's publisher retracted the most-cited study claiming ChatGPT produces large learning gains, a paper referenced in policy documents and vendor pitches worldwide. Meanwhile AI-assisted marking is becoming an unspoken norm among overloaded Australian teachers, and the IEU warned that poorly deployed AI risks students' cognitive development.
signals: The retracted meta-analysis (504 citations, ~500,000 readers) no longer supports any claim built on it; vendor-cited research now deserves heightened scrutiny.
Stanford SCALE's complementary finding: no high-quality causal studies of AI learning outcomes exist in K-12 classrooms.
Australian teachers on 52-hour weeks are using AI to mark and draft feedback, often without any policy framework around them.
The IEU argues AI tools that short-circuit effortful practice undermine the capabilities schools exist to build.
University of Washington research: teacher resistance to AI is often a values question about professional identity, not a skills gap.
actions: Check whether any school strategy documents or vendor pitches cite the retracted study, directly or via secondary sources.
Establish an explicit position on AI-assisted marking and feedback, with transparency to students and parents.
Design staff professional learning to engage values and identity tensions, not just tool skills.

2026-05-03.headline: Deepfake incidents double as regulators act, and the sharpest AI literacy gap turns out to be in primary school
2026-05-03.overview: The eSafety Commissioner urged schools to report AI-generated deepfake incidents after reports more than doubled in 18 months, releasing an updated Toolkit for Schools. New survey data shows primary teachers report the biggest gap in students' ability to recognise AI-generated content, just as AI tools reach primary classrooms. New York City published hard-limit AI guidance for 1.1 million students, and US students will co-write a model AI policy.
signals: eSafety deepfake reports involving under-18s more than doubled in 18 months; three 'nudify' platforms have been removed from the Australian market and criminal offences now apply in some states.
61% of primary teachers say students struggle badly to distinguish AI-generated content, a far higher share than secondary. Capability is arriving before literacy.
NYC's guidance draws hard lines: no AI grading, no AI disciplinary decisions, no biometric collection without strict oversight. A template for enforceable policy.
AASA, MIT and Day of AI will have students co-draft a model AI policy, formalising student voice in governance.
ISNSW's ICT leadership conference put AI strategy at the top of the independent sector's agenda.
actions: Establish a deepfake incident protocol distinct from general cyberbullying policy, using the eSafety toolkit.
Prioritise concrete AI-content literacy in the primary years rather than scaled-down secondary ethics content.
Consider structured student input into the school's next AI policy revision.

2026-04-21.headline: Adoption is outrunning evidence: covert AI marking, thin research foundations, and a call to start with graduate capabilities
2026-04-21.overview: The inaugural briefing lands on a consistent picture: Australian teachers under workload pressure are adopting AI faster than policy or evidence can follow, with some using it covertly to mark. Stanford's review found only 20 rigorous causal studies among more than 800, and the leading advice from the CoSN conference was to anchor AI strategy in what graduates should be able to do, not in tools.
signals: Teachers averaging 52-hour weeks are using AI to manage marking, sometimes in secret, because school policies are silent on staff use.
Stanford SCALE: of 800+ studies on AI in K-12, only 20 support causal claims; tools with pedagogical guardrails outperform answer-generators.
NC State research: AI tutoring does not automatically redistribute teacher attention; help patterns stay 'sticky' without deliberate strategy.
The US has made AI literacy a formal federal grant priority, including detecting AI-generated disinformation.
CoSN 2026: define graduate capabilities first, then work backwards to activities and tools.
actions: Make sure the school AI policy explicitly addresses teacher use for assessment, not just student use.
Ask vendors for causal evidence, not correlational claims, in any procurement conversation.
Anchor the AI strategy to graduate capabilities rather than platforms.
